Summary

Phainon takes Mydei home to meet his parents. His world-renowned, critically-acclaimed parents, Aglaea Mnestia and Anaxagoras Cerces. Mydei does his best not to freak out.

chapters.title: Contingency Plan
chapters.html:
“This song is terrible,” Mydei says, swatting vaguely at the car stereo.

Phainon shoves his hand away and places it back on the wheel. Mydei can hear the smirk in his voice when he says, “That’s what you get for giving me the aux.”

“I can still crash the car.”

“It’s your car. You love this shitty thing.”

Mydei’s car is a two-seater pickup truck that’s about as old as he is. He bought it at a suspiciously low price from a sketchy used car lot when he was seventeen. For his eighteenth birthday his friends pooled their money together and bought the car a pink paint job. “It isn’t shitty,” Mydei says, affronted. “Don’t you dare disrespect Kokopo like that.”

Phainon snorts. He leans back in the passenger’s seat and skips the song. An equally terrible song comes on. Perhaps worse.

“You could at least be grateful,” Mydei mutters. He knows for a fact that Phainon’s music isn’t all this atrocious.

“Yeah, yeah, you’re driving me home for fall break out of the goodness of your bleeding heart. Praise be to your glorious name forevermore,” Phainon says, waving a hand vaguely. He kicks his feet up on the dashboard. “You’re exiting in three miles, by the way.”

“Change the fucking song and maybe I won’t drive you into a ditch.”

Phainon laughs brightly. He taps something on his phone. A new song plays.

“Is this the theme of Dromas Train?” Mydei asks, incredulous. “The kids’ show?”

“Yep,” Phainon says proudly. He lifts his can of cheerwine to his mouth.

Mydei accelerates. The bright red soda spills all over his face.

Phainon splutters. He wipes the drink from his chin with a napkin from the glove compartment.

“You have to get me another napkin,” Mydei says, just to be petty. “Because you used one of mine.”

“You,” Phainon says over the Dromas Train theme song, “are the actual worst.”

Mydei glances over at him. There’s still a single drop of soda on his nose, glimmering like blood. “You know what I want.”

Phainon heaves a dramatic sigh. Then, from the car speakers, Mydei catches the opening of his favorite song. “You’re welcome,” Phainon sniffs, turning up his nose.

“Shut up,” Mydei tells him, full of affection. “This is the best part.”

“The whole song is the best part—”

“I just told you to shut up—”

***

Twenty minutes later Mydei drives them up to a white house with a beautifully maintained succulent garden in front and parks his shitty car next to the gorgeous gold luxury sedan in the driveway. Immediately it strikes him that he is vastly outclassed.

“You didn’t tell me your parents were rich,” Mydei hisses, as he frees Phainon’s suitcase from the truck bed. “I would have dressed up or something.”

Phainon takes the suitcase from him and sets it down on the ground. “Are you worried?” he asks, grinning.

“No,” Mydei lies through his teeth. He throws his duffel bag down at Phainon, who yelps but catches it regardless.

“It’s no big deal,” Phainon calls, as he sets down the duffel. “I mean, Aglaea’s design label is a little famous, I guess. And Anaxa might have, like, fifty papers published, but he’s mostly a professor.”

Mydei’s hands actually go cold. “You don’t mean Aglaea Mnestia,” he says slowly. “And Anaxagoras Cerces.”

“Yeah! You know them already?”

Does he know them, he asks. Of course Mydei knows them. Aglaea Mnestia designed eight Met Gala outfits last year alone. She has her own fragrance line and custom sunglasses line. Anaxagoras Cerces is literally a Nobel Prize winner.

Mydei sits down in the truck bed. He stares up at the sky. He is so fucked.

Phainon climbs up into the truck bed and frowns at the empty space. “Is the cover giving you trouble again?”

“No,” Mydei says weakly, gathering his suddenly feeble courage. Meeting Phainon’s parents. Phainon’s world-renowned, critically-acclaimed parents. Meeting them in his shitty pink twenty-year-old pickup truck.

“Let’s go, then,” Phainon says. He holds out one hand.

Mydei takes it. He gets the sinking feeling, as he approaches the house, that he is leading himself to his doom.

***

“And you must be Mydeimos,” says the most ethereally dressed woman that Mydei has ever seen. “Good afternoon. Aglaea Mnestia. Pleased to make your acquaintance.”

Mydei has both hands full with his duffel bag and his backpack. Thank fuck he wore his nice corduroys today instead of the paint-stained ones. “Just Mydei is fine,” he says, setting down the bags as carefully as possible on the gorgeous hardwood floor. “Nice to meet you too.”

Aglaea stares him right in the eyes. She shakes his hand.

“Thanks for having me,” Mydei says, a little awkwardly.

Aglaea smiles slightly. “Of course. Phainon told me you typically spend holidays alone, so I’m glad to host you. Thanksgiving is for family, right?”

“Family,” a new voice sneers. “What right do you have to claim that?”

From the living room, someone emerges into the foyer, looking him up and down. With one eye. Oh god, it really is Anaxagoras Cerces.

“Hello,” Mydei says. He might be sweating through his shirt.

Anaxa nods at him with a rather pleasant expression. “Hello, Mydei. Lovely to finally meet you.” Then, turning to Aglaea, “You can hardly claim that this holiday is for family when you and I are celebrating it. And with Phainon, no less. Are you trying to spit all over the memory of his biological parents?”

“Are you trying to diminish our role in raising him?” Aglaea asks, just as coldly. “Anaxagoras, be reasonable.”

“Holidays are for all loved ones, not just one’s family—who, mind you, are deceased, for all three of us—”

“Anaxagoras, do not bring his parents into this—”

“Mydei!” Phainon calls from the top of the stairwell. “Are you coming?”

Like magic, Anaxa and Aglaea fall into perfect silence. Even their expressions become totally civil again. Aglaea smiles at him and says, “Please, make yourself at home. Come down for dinner when you’re ready.”

Mydei picks up his bags again. Slowly, he makes his way up the stairs. Sure enough, the moment he’s out of view, he can hear whispers of their voices again. Mydei is too relieved that his first impressions are over to eavesdrop.

Phainon beams when he finally makes it to the bedroom. “Finally!” He rushes over and takes Mydei’s duffel bag from him, plunking it down next to his open suitcase. “Now we have a luggage section. Isn’t it great?”

“A luggage section,” Mydei repeats drily, staring at their stuff. Oddly, the suitcase and the duffel next to each other make his chest feel warm. Like his things belong with Phainon’s. He clears his throat. “That’s the dumbest thing you’ve ever come up with.”

“I thought the chicken pot pie in the tortilla was the worst one?”

Ah. Right. The chicken pot pie in the tortilla. Mydei shudders just to think of it. “Luggage section is the second dumbest thing.”

“Thank you,” Phainon says, vindicated. He flops down on the bed. “Aglaea said she’s ordering dinner. I asked her to get panang beef curry and chicken satay for us to split.”

“And an extra—”

“Extra sweet iced tea for you. I know.”

Mydei sits down on the bed next to him. Of course Phainon knows. Phainon knows him better than anyone. “Thanks.”

“Anytime,” Phainon says, through a wide yawn. “I’m so tired. Should I just take a nap?”

“You’re tired?” Mydei asks, scoffing. “I drove for four hours to get here and I’m doing fine.”

“One of those was just going to Costco.”

“I like Costco,” Mydei says defensively. Then, to his horror, he fails to stifle a yawn.

Phainon cackles.

Mydei turns his head to glare at him. “I’m only yawning because you’re yawning, dumbass.”

“Nope!” Phainon wraps both hands around his waist and drags him down. “We’re both exhausted beyond recognition. It’s naptime. Goodnight.”

“It’s like five in the afternoon.”

“Naptime,” Phainon repeats, with conviction.

Mydei stifles another yawn.

“Just lie down with me,” Phainon pleads. Then he turns his big wide eyes on Mydei.

Mydei makes the world’s most exaggerated sigh and then lies down next to Phainon. He’s not going to fall asleep. He’s just going to lie here… just for a few minutes…

***

Something pokes Mydei’s cheek. He wrinkles his brow and rolls away from it. It returns. Poke. Poke. Poke.

“What,” Mydei grumbles, opening his eyes a sliver. The world is tinted with the bluish haze of sleep. And right in front of him is—

“Hi,” says Phainon, grinning at him.

Mydei blinks the sleep from his eyes. “…Hi,” he says. He tries to sit up.

Tries, because Phainon’s arm is thrown across his lower back. Mydei belatedly realizes he’s lying on top of Phainon, his head pillowed on his chest.

“Don’t leave. I wanna stay here.”

Mydei glares at him. “Then why were you poking me?”

“‘Cause I like annoying you,” Phainon says brightly. “Did it work?”

“Light of my life, pain in my ass,” Mydei mutters. He drags himself up, ignoring Phainon’s whines of protest. It’s easy to overpower a one-handed Phainon, so Mydei pins his other wrist to the bed while he gets up. He stretches out his arms over his head and sighs. He’s sore from sitting in the driver’s seat all day; the release feels good.

Phainon stares at him, his face flushed. His wrist lies limp against the bed where Mydei pinned it.

Mydei throws his sweater at him. “Get up. Dinnertime.”

Phainon turns over and groans into his pillow. “Five minutes.”

It is not five minutes. Phainon takes five just to get up, and then another ten searching through his closet wearing only his boxers. It drives Mydei insane. He takes out his phone and pretends he’s not looking. God. They live together, for fuck’s sake. Mydei sees him in his boxers every day. And yet here he is, still fighting the urge to stare.

Once Phainon is finally dressed, they head downstairs.

“Perfect timing,” says Aglaea, setting down her half-full wine glass. “The order just arrived. Go ahead and serve yourselves. The tom yum is mine; all the other dishes are to share.”

At the bar, Anaxa is arranging the delivery in a row, putting serving utensils in each dish. He glances up at them. “You ordered an extra sweet iced tea.”

“For Mydei,” Phainon says, grabbing the drink. “He’s got a sweet tooth.”

Anaxa looks at him with his single, intimidating eye. “You do.”

His gaze is sharp. Piercing. Mydei might be sweating again. “It’s just a personal preference. I don’t make Phainon eat anything too sweet for his tastes, or anything like that.”

Aglaea raises her eyebrows over the rim of her wire-frame glasses. “You cook?”

“A little,” Mydei says, his nervousness only mounting. “I make dinner most nights.”

“And he makes our breakfast and meal preps our lunch,” Phainon adds dreamily, heaping fried rice onto his plate. “Mydei is the best cook I’ve ever met. So good that I don’t even feel bad about doing all the other chores.”

“You don’t do all of them. I buy groceries.”

“We go grocery shopping together,” Phainon corrects. He grabs a second plate and begins piling more food onto it. “I’m there for moral support.”

“Are you filling my plate?”

“I’m being nice,” Phainon says, holding it out of Mydei’s reach. “You could try it sometime.”

“Maybe I want more chicken.”

“I know what you want,” Phainon says simply. And damn it, he does know what Mydei wants. The plate has exactly the portions Mydei would have served himself.

The dinner table is made of a polished tree trunk section, complete with age rings and a glossy resin finish. Mydei sits down next to Phainon with trepidation. He lifts his fork to his mouth carefully, trying his best to appear… graceful, or whatever. He doesn’t know. Would he be judged for bad utensil etiquette?

“So,” says Anaxa, the last to sit down. “Do you enjoy cooking?”

Mydei nods. “It’s relaxing. And this idiot likes my cooking, so—”

“I love it,” Phainon corrects. He steals Mydei’s drink and takes a sip. He makes a face. “How do you even drink that?”

“It’s not that sweet.” He snatches it back and drinks some himself. It’s full of condensed milk and sugar. Perfect.

Aglaea looks at him with a contemplating sparkle in her eye. Mydei’s heart sinks. It’s the same look Phainon gives him before he has bad ideas. It’s the look he had when he put the chicken pot pie in the tortilla.

And then Aglaea says, “Would you like to cook our Thanksgiving dinner?”

Mydei nearly drops his fork. “What?”

“Anaxagoras and I both hate cooking. In the past, we’ve always bought prepared dishes. But since Phainon speaks so highly of you, I figured I’d offer. I understand if the undertaking is too great.”

Mydei stares at her. “You want me to make your holiday dinner?”

“Only if you like.”

Mydei hesitates. He does like cooking.

“You would, of course, be welcome to use my credit card while shopping. Purchase whatever you need.”

Mydei blinks. He’s changed his mind. Maybe Phainon having rich parents is a good thing. A great thing. Maybe it’s the best thing ever. “I would love to,” he says seriously. “Do you have any requests?”

Aglaea smiles. “I’m so glad. As for specific dishes…” She turns to Anaxa and tilts her head.

“Oh, come off it, Aglaea,” Anaxa drawls. For the first time, Mydei notices his empty plate. He’s not even drinking wine with Aglaea—he’s only drinking water, and slowly at that. “You know damn well it won’t make a difference.”

“Don’t be rude,” she says, her eyes narrowing. “It’s Thanksgiving; you’ll have to eat something. Food, you fool, not nutritional supplements. Just choose a dish you can tolerate.”

Anaxa glares at her with double the venom packed into his single eye. “You know my appetite is nonexistent on the best of days. Rather than catering to the useless preferences of a lost cause, why not provide your own preferences? You’ll actually eat the dinner—”

“I was hoping that you would eat it as well, dear,” says Aglaea, with the most threatening smile Mydei has ever seen.

Anaxa sighs. “Watermelon radish,” he says finally. “I can eat watermelon radish.”

Mydei’s mouth is full of panang beef curry. He’s been silently racing Phainon to see who can finish first. “Okay,” he says, once he’s finally finished his bite of beef. “I'll make sure to include a watermelon radish dish.”

When he looks back down, Phainon’s plate is empty already.

“I win,” Phainon whispers, grinning sideways at him.

Mydei kicks him under the table.

***

“Come back to bed,” Phainon pleads, reaching out lazily with both hands.

Mydei surrenders his left hand to Phainon’s reach, but nothing more. “I have to plan a menu. It’s already six thirty. Time to wake up.”

Phainon groans. He pulls Mydei’s left hand, to no avail. He’s still half-asleep, his grip weak. When his hands threaten to slip, Mydei holds onto him to keep their contact.

“You can go back to sleep. I’ll turn down the lights.”

“I won’t sleep unless you’re back.”

Mydei looks up from his menu notes. “You sleep without me most nights.”

“Only because I know you’re next door,” Phainon mumbles. He rolls his face into the pillow and tugs on Mydei’s hand one last time.

Mydei ignores him. He scribbles out another rejected side dish: crab mashed potatoes. Too pretentious.

Phainon drags himself to a sitting position. “Is it really that important? It’s just dinner. I’ll even help you cook.”

“You stay the fuck out of my kitchen,” Mydei says, out of habit. Then he sighs, running his hands through his hair. “I just… I want to make a good impression.”

“You already have.” Phainon gets up and wraps his arms around Mydei’s shoulders from behind. “When we go shopping later today, I’ll help you decide. Bring the whole list.”

Mydei exhales. He tips his head up to look back at Phainon. “I’m blaming you if anything goes wrong.”

Phainon laughs quietly. “Yeah, of course. Now come back to bed. It’s six thirty. Too early.”

Mydei is usually up by six thirty. Phainon is usually up by seven. But they’re on vacation, Mydei reminds himself. And they’ve got nothing to do. No deadlines to meet.

“Fine,” Mydei mutters, and he lets Phainon drag him back into his bed. Mydei’s head is still full of recipes and dishes and shopping plans, but the soft rustling of Phainon’s breath in his hair is enough to make his thoughts slow down to a reasonable pace. He doesn’t fall back asleep—he doubts Phainon does either—but it’s nice, resting alongside him.

This is why, despite everything—the fights, the idiocy, the chicken pot pie in the tortilla—Mydei still chooses to be by his side. He’s never liked the quiet when he’s alone, but with Phainon, the quiet is soft, welcoming. With Phainon, the quiet is alright.

***

“So the sweet potatoes have to go in the oven in a few minutes, and the stuffing and the pork roast are already baking, and the fish is going into the soup to simmer in ten minutes. Then after the fish, the clams go in, and then the prawns. Are you done with the corn yet?”

Phainon, who is sitting on the kitchen floor on a giant pile of newspaper, looks up at him reproachfully. “Of course I’m done with the corn,” he says, affronted. “My sister used to hand me all the corn and make me shuck her portion while she played Dress to Impress.”

Mydei leans down to take the corn from him. He’s shucked all ten ears of corn to perfection. His smile is proud. There’s corn silk in his hair.

“Good job,” Mydei says.

Predictably, Phainon lights up. The corn silk in his hair catches the light. Mydei stifles a laugh and puts the corn into the pot.

“You didn’t need to make this many dishes.”

“Aglaea didn’t give me a budget.”

Phainon raises his eyebrows knowingly. “Is that why you’re making this seafood soup? ‘Cause you’re not on a broke college budget anymore?”

“It’s called cioppino, Phainon. And no. I’m making it because I like seafood.” Also because he looked up Anaxagoras Cerces, and his Wikipedia page said he was born and raised in the city where cioppino was invented. If he scores some points with his research, all the better. And all on Aglaea’s credit card. Triple win.

“Sweet potato time,” Phainon reminds him.

“I thought I told you to stay out of my kitchen,” Mydei grumbles, but puts the tray of sweet potatoes into the oven regardless.

“You told me to shuck corn. You never said where. Anyway, give me another task. I’m ready.”

Mydei heaves a world-weary sigh. “You can take the tails off the prawns.”

Phainon groans. “More manual labor,” he sighs, flopping back against the corn-covered newspaper. The corn silk in his hair gains several new friends. “Mydei, can’t you give me another task? I could stir the soup. Or—or just watch the soup!”

Mydei rolls his eyes. “On second thought, go take a shower.”

“Or set your timers!” Phainon calls from the hallway. “I could set your timers!”

Mydei scoffs. Good thing there’s no one else in the kitchen to see him grin into the soup pot as he dumps in the fish.

***

Just as Mydei is pulling the cioppino off the stove, the doorbell rings.

“Hyacine!” Phainon calls from down the hall, sounding delighted. He reappears in the entryway, hair freshly de-corn-silked, and throws open the door. Then he pauses. “And—Cas?”

Mydei does a double take. Sure enough, Castorice is standing in the foyer. Castorice, his freshman year roommate. Castorice, who goes to the same college he and Phainon do. “What are you doing here?”

Castorice gives him a polite little wave. “Hi, Mydei. I grew up down the street. Our families usually celebrate holidays together.”

Phainon practically tackles her into a hug. “You should have driven with us!”

“My car only has two seats,” Mydei reminds him.

“Well, Cas could have had shotgun, and I could have family dogged it.”

Four seconds of complete silence. Everyone looks at Phainon.

“You know,” says Phainon. “Like when you sit in the truck bed. Family dog.”

“…Anyway,” says Castorice. She and Mydei share a look. Sometimes the best way to deal with Phainon is to gloss over his Phainon-isms. “Nice to see you again, Mydei. I suppose you’re here as Phainon’s guest?”

Mydei nods.

“Ah, and I’m Hyacine Aquila,” says the other woman. She gives him a radiant smile. “Hello! Nice to meet you! I’m the Professor’s TA.”

“You were invited because you’re his TA?” Mydei asks, a little baffled.

“He always invites me to family holidays! It’s because I was raised in a cult.”

Mydei waits for her to elaborate. She doesn’t.

“Well, how can I help?” Castorice asks, coming into the kitchen. “It looks like you’re almost done. If there are any last tasks, I’ll be glad to assist.”

Everything’s coming together; the pork roast is resting on the counter, and the sweet potatoes are almost done. The corn and the cioppino are both done, sitting on the stove, and the stuffing is being kept warm in the oven. All that’s left is—

“You can help slice the watermelon radish, if you want.”

Castorice nods and gets to work.

“If you’re close to done, can I help prepare the dishes?” Hyacine asks. “I can set out plates and silverware for us all.”

“Perfect.”

“I can do something too,” Phainon offers eagerly. Mydei swears he can see the ears perked up in his still-damp hair.

“No,” Mydei says.

“Please?”

“No.”

“Pleeease?”

Mydei heaves a sigh. He throws something at Phainon.

Phainon yelps and dodges it. “HEY—wait.” He leans down and picks it up off the ground. “Is this one of the brownies you made last weekend?”

“No,” Mydei says flatly. “It’s a Frisbee.”

Phainon beams and unseals the plastic bag. He takes a huge bite of the brownie. “You love me,” he says, grinning at Mydei. “You made them with dark chocolate and lower sugar. For me.”

“Can’t hear you,” Mydei calls to him. “I’m too busy eating all your sweet potatoes before you can have any.”

Phainon obediently shuts his mouth. He eats the brownie in silence.

While Castorice finishes slicing up the watermelon radishes, Mydei stands next to her, cutting up cucumber and red onions. He’s cooked alongside Castorice before; in freshman year, she was often making late-night instant ramen while he was preparing his pre-workout breakfast. The last dish comes together quickly with both of them working on it: a watermelon radish salad, complete with feta cheese and grated ginger.

And then, finally, the dinner is complete.

“Happy Thanksgiving, everyone,” Aglaea declares, standing at the head of the dining table. “We’re glad to have you all here for this celebration of loved ones.”

Anaxa looks over at her. He opens his mouth.

Mydei nearly breaks out into a cold sweat. Are they really going to fight on a holiday? He gets that they have a weird dynamic, but—

“You’ve all enriched our lives over the last year,” Anaxa says. “And we hope you’ll be a part of them for many years to come.”

Aglaea actually smiles at him. She clinks her glass against Anaxa’s. “To our continued happiness.”

Anaxa’s mouth turns up at the corner. “To our continued happiness.”

Shockingly civil. So civil, in fact, that Mydei actually looks at their hands for the first time, and notices their matching rings. Wedding rings. Maybe they actually like each other.

“Let us begin,” Aglaea declares, and then the feast starts.

Mydei has personally tasted every dish on the table. He knows they’re excellent. But it’s still gratifying to see the way Phainon’s eyes light up when he takes three pieces of corn on the cob and grabs the largest sweet potato. It’s still gratifying to see Aglaea serve herself another piece of pork roast, and to see Hyacine’s eyes light up when she tries the stuffing, and to see Castorice satisfied with their work on the watermelon radish salad.

This is what he cooks for, above all else: making people happy. Even Anaxa, who’s only eaten the watermelon radishes, seems to be doing alright.

That is, until someone passes him the soup.

“Is this cioppino?” Anaxa asks.

Mydei sits up straighter. “Yeah,” he says. “I made it with prawns and clams, but no squid.”

“Hm,” says Anaxa. He looks at Mydei, his expression unreadable. He ladles himself a bowl of cioppino.

“If you don’t eat it all, I won’t be offended,” Mydei says, a little panicked. He didn’t expect that Anaxa would eat anything but the watermelon radish. After all, he rarely eats anything. He just takes his nutrition supplements and calls it a day.

Anaxa takes a sip of the soup. He takes another. Then he tips the bowl up to his mouth and actually drinks the entire thing.

“Is it good?” Mydei asks, like an idiot.

Anaxa looks down at the empty bowl. Then he looks at Mydei. “My sister used to make cioppino for me,” he says quietly. “When she passed, I thought I’d never have it again.”

“Oh,” says Mydei. “I’m sorry.”

“This,” says Anaxa, “tastes like what she used to make for me.” Then, as he refills his bowl, “Thank you.”

Mydei sits there at the table with his idiot roommate, his less-idiot former roommate, a girl who was apparently raised in a cult, the dress designer of the century, and Nobel Prize winner Anaxagoras Cerces. He looks down at the dinner he made for all of them. The joy they’re all sharing. “Yeah,” he says, letting himself smile. “Of course.”

Then Castorice passes him the pork roast, and he digs in.

***

He and Phainon are preparing to leave on Saturday morning when Aglaea and Anaxa approach him outside by his car.

“You’ll make a good match for him,” Aglaea says, apropos of nothing. “I had my doubts when he told me you fought frequently, but it appears my worries were unfounded.”

Anaxa scoffs and leans against the outer wall. “As if you have any room to comment on frequent fights.”

“You have even less, Anaxagoras.” Then, turning back to Mydei, she says quite pleasantly, “Your dinner was lovely, and your company even more so. You’re welcome back for the winter holidays, if you’d like to join us.”

Mydei blinks, surprised. “Thank you,” he says, caught off guard. “I’m glad you think well of me. You’re both very important to Phainon.”

Aglaea smiles. “You have our approval.”

Mydei feels his face heat up faintly. It sounds a little—well, it sounds a little like—

“Ah, right. I have this for you as well,” Aglaea says, holding out a small box in her palm.

Mydei opens it. It’s a gorgeous ring, set with a small diamond encased in golden sun rays.

“Audata’s engagement ring,” Anaxa explains. “Phainon’s biological mother. This is one of their only remaining possessions. You’ll most likely want to get your own wedding rings, but it would mean a lot to Phainon if you proposed with this one.”

Mydei stares at the engagement ring. “If I… WHAT??”

“Proposed,” Aglaea says. “With this ring.”

Mydei feels a little lightheaded. “We’re just roommates,” he says weakly. “Phainon and I aren’t even dating. We just—we just live together. And he just made me drive him here. We’re not getting married.”

Both of them look at him in silence.

“We’re really not,” Mydei repeats desperately. “I’m just his friend. Or, like, his rival or something. We’re just—we’re just Mydei and Phainon. I don’t know.”

Aglaea smiles knowingly. She presses the ring into his hands. “Keep it anyway,” she says. “I have a feeling you’ll need it someday.”

“MYDEI!” Phainon yells from inside the house. He stumbles down the front steps under the weight of all their combined luggage. “Help me out before I collapse and die.”

“Stop whining,” Mydei yells back. “I’m getting the truck bed ready.”

“Get it ready faster!”

“You have to promise you’ll only play good songs.”

“I promise,” Phainon says solemnly. “All Dromas Train, all the way home.”

Mydei sighs. Quietly, before Phainon can see, he pockets the ring.

“I think I will need it,” he says to Aglaea. “Unfortunately.”

Phainon clambers into the passenger seat next to him. He puts his feet up on the dashboard and leans against the closed door. “What was that about?” he asks. “Need what?”

“Nothing,” Mydei says. He puts the keys in the ignition. “Come on. Let’s go home.”
